source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) training slide deck, "Rice and Environment" (ដំណំស្រូវនិងបរិស្ថាន), no elibrary URL visible on the scan
text:
Rice growth depends on four environmental factors working together: water, temperature, sunlight, and wind/humidity. Understanding each factor's needs at different growth stages helps farmers time planting and anticipate problems.

WATER: Rainwater is the main way rice gets the freshwater it needs to dissolve soil nutrients for root uptake, and water also supplies the carbon dioxide used in photosynthesis (6 CO2 + 6 H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2 under sunlight and chlorophyll). Nearly all rice ecosystems need at least 1,000-2,000 mm of rainfall spread across the growing season. Cambodia's rice systems fall into three main types based on water regime: rainfed upland rice (ស្រូវចំការ), rainfed lowland rice with early/medium/late maturity groups (ស្រូវតំបន់ទំនាប), and deepwater/floating rice (ស្រូវឡើងទឹក).

TEMPERATURE: Rice needs a temperature range appropriate to its growth stage and elevation; because temperature swings with the seasons and with how close an area is to the equator, different farming regions in Cambodia experience different heat exposure along the north-south gradient. The general optimal range for rice growth and tillering is about 25-30°C. If temperature drops to around 12°C and stays there for 6-7 days during the flowering stage, it can cause up to 100% sterility (empty grains). Below is a stage-by-stage guide to temperature tolerance (illustrative ranges, not exact lookup values):
- Germination: minimum ~10°C, maximum ~45°C, optimum 20-25°C
- Seedling growth: minimum ~13°C, maximum ~35°C, optimum 25-30°C
- Tillering: minimum ~9-16°C, maximum ~33°C, optimum 25-31°C
- Root elongation: minimum ~24°C, optimum around 25°C
- Panicle initiation: minimum ~15-20°C, maximum ~38°C, optimum 25-30°C
- Heading: minimum ~15-20°C, maximum ~30°C, optimum 25-31°C
- Flowering: minimum ~22°C, maximum ~35-36°C, optimum 30-33°C
- Ripening (milk stage): minimum ~17°C, maximum ~38°C
- Ripening (dough/maturity stage): minimum ~19°C, maximum ~30°C, optimum 20-25°C
- Overall ripening period: minimum ~12-18°C, maximum ~30°C, optimum ~23°C

SUNLIGHT: Rice needs strong sunlight (feugh sunlight/direct radiation) throughout its growth, and especially during two critical windows. For high yield overall, rice needs at least about 250 calories per square centimeter per day. During the panicle-formation and ripening stages specifically, rice needs roughly 350 calories per square centimeter per day. If sunlight intensity drops sharply during ripening, it delays grain filling, increases the number of unfilled/chalky grains (the rice equivalent of empty husks), and can lead to more disease problems.

DAY LENGTH (photoperiod): The best day length for rice cultivation overall is about 8-12 hours of daylight. Day lengths longer than about 15 hours can delay flowering, particularly for photoperiod-sensitive (rdouv kaal-sensitive) varieties. Farmers growing photoperiod-sensitive varieties should be aware that unusually long daylight hours late in the season can push back the flowering date.

WIND AND HUMIDITY: Wind is an important climate factor for rice because it plays a role in dispersing heat around the plant canopy and helps carry away excess heat that builds up around the leaves. Wind also assists nutrient uptake from the environment by helping the photosynthesis and respiration processes exchange gases with the leaf surface. However, if wind is too strong during the flowering stage, it can cut short pollination time and cause the grain to fail to fill properly, as well as promote lodging (plants falling over) and disease spread. Optimal wind speed for rice is around 0.75-2.25 meters per second. Optimal relative humidity for rice is 60-80%; humidity that is too high can encourage disease and pest problems, while humidity that is too low can cause faster water loss and leaf drying (desiccation) in the crop.

SOIL AND NUTRIENT FACTORS: Soil pH strongly affects how well rice can take up the natural mineral nutrients present in the soil, so it's one of the biggest soil-based influences on rice growth. Rice can absorb both macronutrients and micronutrients — 16 different nutrient elements in total — in various chemical forms. Two soil problems farmers should watch for: (1) acid sulfate soils and heavily leached/bleached soils, where very low sodium (Na) and low nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) levels can cut yield by as much as 50%, combined with iron (Fe) and aluminum (Al) toxicity; and (2) correcting soils that are too acidic on the surface, which can be done using limestone powder (dolomite/agricultural lime) or copper sulfate (CuSO4).
caveat: Temperature, sunlight, and wind figures are presented as illustrative ranges from a MAFF extension slide deck (source PDF has no visible elibrary URL), not exact scientific lookup values — treat them as general guidance rather than precise thresholds for a specific field. The stage-by-stage temperature table in the source combines minimum/maximum/optimum figures across several growth stages in a compact table; figures here are transcribed as clearly as the source allows, but for critical timing decisions (e.g. flowering-stage cold-damage risk), cross-check against a current CARDI or IRRI reference where possible.
